More Details in Beacon Murder

by Leonard Sparks August 30, 2026 Why you can trust The Current

Convicted couple appeals life sentences

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:42
Instaread

A woman sentenced this month with her husband to life in a federal prison for the death of her ex-husband in Beacon described finding him dead in the basement of her Church Street apartment and her children riding in the family SUV with their father’s body in the back.

That trip to Amsterdam, northwest of Albany, is one of the details Jamie Orsini reveals in a handwritten letter pleading with federal Judge Philip Halpern for a lighter sentence following the convictions of her and her husband, Nicholas Orsini, in the death of Steven Kraft. He has not been seen since April 28, 2020, when, after a custody visit, he dropped the two daughters he shares with Jamie Orsini off at 10 W. Church St. in Beacon, where she lived with Nicholas Orsini and the children.

Both Orsinis, who were arrested in 2023 after moving to Amsterdam, filed notices to appeal their convictions and punishments — life with the possibility of parole on the carjacking charge; up to five years on a charge of participating in a conspiracy to commit carjacking, to run concurrently; and $6,435 in restitution. Jamie Orsini, 38, filed notice on the day of her sentencing; Nicholas Orsini, 36, filed on Aug. 20, a week after his sentencing.

Jamie Orsini wrote the letter, which became public on Aug. 26, before Halpern sentenced her on Aug. 11, and Nicholas Orsini on Aug. 13, to life in prison on a federal charge — carjacking resulting in death — in the killing of Kraft, who disappeared six weeks before a court hearing in his effort to seek sole custody of his daughters or greater visitation.

Blaming her current husband, Jamie Orsini claimed that she only learned of Kraft’s death when she saw his body in the basement of the apartment. “Steven had a gash to the head, there was blood everywhere, and I saw a silver hammer-like object covered in blood next to where Nicholas stood,” she told Halpern.

Nicholas Orsini threatened to kill her and the children, Jamie Orsini alleges, so she followed his instructions to cover up the killing. That included sending the text message to Kraft’s phone that prosecutors said was meant to create the impression that she was unaware of his death, said Orsini.

Prosecutors also obtained security footage and a receipt showing that two days before Kraft disappeared, Jamie Orsini used cash to buy a 10-foot-by-100-foot tarp, duct tape, painters’ coveralls and galvanized trash cans from the Home Depot on Route 9 in Fishkill. In her letter, she said Nicholas Orsini told her to buy the items, which prosecutors allege were used to dispose of Kraft’s body, because he had agreed to paint the front of 10 W. Church St. in exchange for reduced rent.

With Kraft’s body in the back of the SUV, Jamie Orsini said she and the children rode the next day with Nicholas Orsini to Amsterdam, where the Orsinis attended high school. Along Covey Road in Amsterdam, he “dragged” Kraft’s body out of the car to bury it, Jamie Orsini claims.

She left her husband for an hour, then returned to Covey Road to retrieve him for the trip back to Beacon, according to the letter. Back in Beacon, Nicholas Orsini “burned evidence along with our regular garbage in a homemade burn bin,” she said.

Although “there were many times” she wanted to “speak out” about what she knew, Jamie Orsini said she didn’t because of advice from previous lawyers. Prosecutors and police were “not willing” to talk to her, she said, and she feared that “what happened to Steven” would happen to her and her children.

“There are things that I’ve done well and things I’ve done horribly wrong,” she wrote. “Things I have done terribly wrong include not immediately reporting truthfully to the police that my current husband murdered my ex-husband.”

The couple, who met in a high school art class and later reunited through Facebook, were initially united in their denial of killing Kraft, but now blame each other for his death.

In a letter to Halpern on July 14, the attorneys for Nicholas Orsini said their client, following his conviction, had “voluntarily led law enforcement to the location in Amsterdam where he believed he had buried Mr. Kraft’s remains. Although the search was unsuccessful, that effort — undertaken without any promise of benefit and at his own initiative — reflects a recognition of responsibility and a sincere, if belated, attempt to provide the Kraft family with some measure of closure.”

They added that prosecutors had “acknowledged, at least informally, that Jamie Orsini was the driving force behind the offense and that Nicholas Orsini was not the primary instigator.” The defense told Halpern that Jamie Orsini had convinced her husband that “Kraft was sexually assaulting their nonverbal autistic daughter in the bathrooms of the fast-food restaurants where his supervised visitation took place.”

Nicholas Orsini’s mother, aunt, four sisters, brother-in-law and a lifelong friend wrote the judge to ask for leniency. Their letters, Nicholas Orsini’s attorney said, establish “a consistent and detailed picture of a relationship defined by psychological control, financial exploitation, physical abuse and deliberate isolation.”

They also cited as mitigating factors the fact that Nicholas Orsini’s parents divorced when he was 10 and said he had been sexually abused by the friend of a sister. But Jamie Orsini’s portrait of her husband is less sympathetic.

She told Halpern that she has spent “my life being abused,” including by Kraft and Nicholas Orsini. “I am a good mother and a good person,” she told Halpern. “Please don’t define me by the men I’ve picked.”
